preacher.name: John Wesley
preacher.role: Anglican priest, evangelist and leader of Methodism
preacher.bio: John Wesley was born at Epworth, Lincolnshire, on 17 June 1703 (Old Style; 28 June New Style). He was educated at Charterhouse and Christ Church, Oxford, became a Fellow of Lincoln College in 1726, and was ordained priest in the Church of England in 1728. At Oxford he led the 'Holy Club', whose members were nicknamed Methodists, and in 1735 he sailed to Georgia, where he ministered at Savannah before returning to England in 1738. On 24 May 1738, at a society meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, he recorded that he felt his heart 'strangely warmed'. In 1739 he followed George Whitefield's example of open-air preaching, beginning at Bristol, and he organised Methodist societies, lay preachers and, from 1744, annual conferences. He meant the movement to stay within the Church of England. He died in London on 2 March 1791.
preacher.corpus_note: The Bicentennial Edition of The Works of John Wesley (Sermons, vols. 1–4, ed. Albert C. Outler; Abingdon, 1984–) numbers the sermon texts 1–151. Its digital branch, the Wesley Works Digitization Project, says it has the texts of all of Wesley's sermons (vols. 1–4) online. Thomas Jackson's 1872 edition of the Works numbers 141 sermons. The Wesley Works Editorial Project's register (compiled by G. P. Van Buskirk, 2016) identifies four of those as by other authors: Charles Wesley, Benjamin Calamy, William Tilly and John Gambold.

sermons.title: The Circumcision of the Heart
sermons.occasion: University sermon on the Feast of the Circumcision
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 2 (1748), where it opens the volume; Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 17; Bicentennial Works 1:398–414
sermons.summary: Wesley defines the 'circumcision of the heart' as the settled disposition Scripture calls holiness: being cleansed from sin and renewed after the mind of Christ. He names its parts as humility, faith, hope and, above all, love of God and neighbour, and calls hearers to make God the single aim of every desire. He then draws reflections from this that serve as a rule by which listeners can judge whether their own hearts have been changed in this way.
sermons.context: According to the Bicentennial editor, Wesley's diaries show he spent close to thirty hours writing a first draft, then about as much time again consulting others on refining it, including his brother Charles and the Rector of Lincoln, Euseby Isham. The editor records Wesley's note that the sermon found favour with the Rector and the Vice-Chancellor, while Thomas Wilson called it 'enthusiastic'. In a letter to John Newton of 14 May 1765, Wesley said the sermon 'contains all that I now teach concerning salvation from all sin, and loving God with an undivided heart'.
sermons.key_line: Circumcision of heart implies humility, faith, hope, and charity.

sermons.title: On Love
sermons.occasion: Sunday preaching in Savannah; Quinquagesima Sunday, whose Epistle is 1 Corinthians 13
sermons.published_in: Arminian Magazine XX (1797), 371–78, published after Wesley's death by George Story; Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 139; Bicentennial Works Sermon 149 (4:378–388)
sermons.summary: Wesley argues that giving away all one's goods to the poor, or even dying as a martyr, profits nothing without love. He defines that love as love of God for his own sake and of all people for God's sake, and uses Paul's list of love's marks as tests for his hearers. He concludes that without love nothing can make life happy or death comfortable.
sermons.context: Wesley's manuscript is annotated in his hand 'Preached, Savannah, Feb. 20, 1736/37', during his ministry in Georgia. George Story first printed it in 1797 and admitted adding sentences of his own. According to the Bicentennial editor, the manuscript surfaced again in 1938, but six of its twelve sheets are lost.
sermons.key_line: And, First, without love nothing can so profit us as to make our lives happy.

sermons.title: Salvation by Faith
sermons.occasion: University sermon before the University of Oxford on the Festival of St Barnabas
sermons.published_in: Separate pamphlet, London, 1738; Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 1 (1746), first sermon; Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 1; Bicentennial Works 1:109–130
sermons.summary: Wesley argues that every blessing comes from God's undeserved grace and that sinners are saved through faith. Saving faith is not the belief of a heathen or of the devil, nor the faith the apostles had while Christ was still on earth; it is trust in the merits of Christ's life, death and resurrection. The salvation it brings is present, a deliverance from the guilt and power of sin. He ends by answering objections that the doctrine undermines holiness, breeds pride or despair, is uncomfortable, or should not be preached.
sermons.context: The Bicentennial editor says Oxford had set this date for Wesley's turn as university preacher soon after his return from Georgia. In the months before, he had tested his message of 'salvation by faith alone' in London churches and, the editor notes, was barred from several pulpits. The sermon came less than three weeks after his Aldersgate experience of 24 May 1738, and the editor calls it his first public evangelical manifesto after Aldersgate. Mark K. Olson notes it was first released in London by the autumn of 1738; it stands first in the first volume of Wesley's Sermons on Several Occasions (1746).
sermons.key_line: For there is nothing we are, or have, or do, which can deserve the least thing at God's hand.

sermons.title: Free Grace
sermons.published_in: Free Grace: A Sermon Preach'd at Bristol (Bristol: S. and F. Farley, 1739); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 128; Bicentennial Works Sermon 110 (3:542–563)
sermons.summary: Wesley argues that God's grace is 'free in all', resting on no human merit, and 'free for all' people. He attacks predestination (unconditional election and reprobation) on several grounds: it makes preaching useless; it weakens holiness, comfort and zeal for good works; it sets Scripture against itself; and it misrepresents the character of Christ and of God. He ends by appealing to God's stated will that no one should perish.
sermons.context: According to the Bicentennial editor, Wesley drew lots on 26 April 1739 on whether to confine his attack on predestination to preaching, and the lot fell on 'preach and print'. He then published the sermon at Bristol. The editor says it marked a breach with George Whitefield that was never more than partly healed. Whitefield answered it in a public letter dated 24 December 1740. Wesley never put it in his collected Sermons, though it ran to ten or eleven separate editions in his lifetime.
sermons.key_line: The grace or love of God, whence cometh our salvation, is free in all, and free for all.

sermons.title: The Almost Christian
sermons.occasion: University sermon before the University of Oxford on the Feast of St James the Apostle
sermons.published_in: First edition, 1741; Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 1 (1746); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 2; Bicentennial Works 1:131–141
sermons.summary: Wesley contrasts the 'almost Christian', who has outward honesty, religious observance and even sincerity, with the 'altogether Christian'. The second is marked by a love of God that fills the heart, a love of every neighbour including enemies, and the faith from which both spring. He presses his hearers to ask which of the two they are.
sermons.context: Wesley's Journal records a sermon on the same text at Charles Square, London, on 28 June 1741. The Bicentennial editor says he revised it with an application aimed at Oxford, where he confessed that the 'almost' state had been his own there. John Gambold had warned him that Oxford hearers were prejudiced against him. The editor states that no record of the sermon's reception survives.
sermons.key_line: Nor may we in any wise except our enemies or the enemies of God and their own souls.

sermons.title: Scriptural Christianity
sermons.occasion: University sermon before the University of Oxford on St Bartholomew's Day
sermons.published_in: Separate pamphlet, 1744; Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 1 (1746); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 4; Bicentennial Works 1:159–180
sermons.summary: Wesley argues that the Spirit's lasting gift to all believers is not miraculous powers but the mind of Christ and the fruit of the Spirit. He traces this Christianity as it starts in individuals, spreads from person to person, and will one day fill the earth. In his closing application he asks whether Oxford's magistrates, heads of colleges, fellows and students show this Christianity, and calls them to repentance.
sermons.context: The Vice-Chancellor sent for Wesley's notes. William Blackstone, in a letter of 28 August 1744, summarised the sermon's charges against the University disapprovingly and said Wesley would be punished 'by a mortifying neglect'. Wesley's Journal for that day reads: 'I preached, I suppose the last time, at St. Mary's.' In 1781 he wrote that the University afterwards paid others to preach in his turn.
sermons.key_line: It was therefore, for a more excellent purpose than this, that "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost."

sermons.title: Justification by Faith
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 1 (1746); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 5; Bicentennial Works 1:181–199
sermons.summary: Wesley grounds justification in humanity's creation in God's image, its fall in Adam, and its redemption through Christ as the 'Second Adam'. He argues that justification is not being made actually righteous, which is sanctification, but God's pardon: the forgiveness of sins. It is given to the ungodly on the single condition of faith.
sermons.context: The Journal records Wesley's first oral sermon on this text on 28 May 1738 at the chapel in Long Acre, London. The Bicentennial editor counts at least eight more uses of the text before 8 June 1742, when he preached on it at Epworth. The written sermon was first published in 1746 and was not reprinted separately in his lifetime.
sermons.key_line: The plain scriptural notion of justification is pardon, the forgiveness of sins.

sermons.title: Upon Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse VI
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 2 (1748); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 26; Bicentennial Works 1:572–591
sermons.summary: Wesley explains that Christ requires a pure intention toward God in works of mercy, such as almsgiving, and works of piety, such as prayer; done to be seen by others, they lose their worth. He then explains the Lord's Prayer petition by petition. On 'forgive us our trespasses', he argues that God forgives us on condition that, and to the degree that, we forgive others from the heart.
sermons.context: This is the sixth of thirteen discourses on Matthew 5–7 that Wesley published in 1748–1750. The Bicentennial editor describes them as separate sermons drawn from material going back to 1725. He also cites Benjamin Ingham's Journal record that during the voyage to Georgia aboard the Simmonds, Wesley went through the Sermon on the Mount with the ship's company.
sermons.key_line: All our trespasses and sins are forgiven us, if we forgive, and as we forgive, others.

sermons.title: Catholic Spirit
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 3 (1750); reissued separately in 1755 and 1770; Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 39; Bicentennial Works 2:79–96
sermons.summary: Wesley argues that differences of opinion and forms of worship may prevent outward union among Christians but need not prevent union in love. The question 'Is thine heart right?' concerns faith in Christ and love of God and of all people, enemies included, not opinions or ways of worship. 'Give me thine hand' means love me, pray for me, spur me to good works and work alongside me. He separates this 'catholic spirit' from indifference to doctrine, worship or church membership.
sermons.context: The Bicentennial editor records only three other preachings on 2 Kings 10:15: 23 November 1740, and 8 September and 3 November 1749. The sermon was reissued separately in 1755 and 1770 with Charles Wesley's hymn 'Catholic Love' added. The editor describes it as Wesley's most formal statement of his non-dogmatic approach to Christian unity.
sermons.key_line: Though we can't think alike, may we not love alike?

sermons.title: The Great Assize
sermons.occasion: Assize sermon before Sir Edward Clive, Judge of Common Pleas, arranged by the High Sheriff, William Cole
sermons.published_in: Published separately in 1758 at the request of the High Sheriff, William Cole, and others; added to Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 1 (1771 edition); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 15; Bicentennial Works 1:354–375
sermons.summary: Using the court before him as a comparison, Wesley describes the events he expected to come before the Last Judgment. He then describes the judgment itself, where every person's deeds, words and even thoughts will be laid open, and what follows: the carrying out of the sentence, the burning of the present earth, and new heavens and a new earth. He applies the theme to the judges and officers present and to the whole assembly, urging them to prepare through repentance and faith.
sermons.context: Wesley's Journal for 27 February 1758 records that he withdrew to Lewisham to write a sermon for the Bedford assizes. The Journal also says the judge invited him to dine after the sermon, but he declined because he had no time and had to set out. The Bicentennial editor calls it Wesley's only published sermon addressed to a civil court. In 1778 Wesley wrote that he could not write a better sermon on the Great Assize than he had then.
sermons.key_line: O make proof of his mercy, rather than his justice; of his love, rather than the thunder of his power!

sermons.title: The Cure of Evil-Speaking
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 4 (1760); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 49; Bicentennial Works 2:251–262
sermons.summary: Wesley defines evil-speaking as telling the real faults of someone who is not present, even when every word is true, and notes how common and well disguised it is. As its cure he sets out Christ's three steps: speak to the offender alone in a spirit of love and humility, then with one or two others, and only then tell the church. He urges Methodists to make 'he censures no man behind his back' their distinguishing mark.
sermons.context: On 29 January 1752 the Wesley brothers and eleven colleagues signed a compact, written in John's hand, not to listen to or pass on ill reports about one another. The Bicentennial editor records Wesley preaching against evil-speaking at least nine times in 1752. The written sermon's only publication in his lifetime was in the fourth volume of Sermons on Several Occasions.
sermons.key_line: All a man says may be as true as the Bible; and yet the saying of it is evil-speaking.

sermons.title: The Use of Money
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. 4 (1760), closing sermon; Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 50; Bicentennial Works 2:263–280
sermons.summary: Wesley treats money as a trust from God, held by stewards, and reduces its right use to three rules. First, gain all you can by honest work without harming your own or your neighbour's body or soul. Second, save all you can by refusing to spend on mere self-gratification. Third, give all you can: provide for yourself and your household, then do good to fellow believers and to all people, since everything belongs to God.
sermons.context: The Bicentennial editor notes that this sermon completes the set later named in the 1763 Model Deed as 'the first four volumes of sermons'. He also counts at least twenty-seven recorded oral sermons by Wesley on Luke 16:9 between 1741 and 1758. According to the editor, Wesley later complained that his warnings went unheeded as Methodists prospered, and his own people did not follow his rejection of accumulating surplus wealth.
sermons.key_line: Having, First, gained all you can, and, Secondly saved all you can, Then "give all you can."

sermons.title: The Scripture Way of Salvation
sermons.published_in: First published 1765; added to Sermons on Several Occasions in the 1771 edition; Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 43; Bicentennial Works 2:153–169
sermons.summary: Wesley defines the salvation of Ephesians 2:8 as a present reality. It runs from the first workings of prevenient ('preventing') grace, through justification and sanctification, to entire sanctification. He describes faith as a divine evidence and conviction of things not seen, and argues that it is the only condition immediately necessary for both justification and sanctification, with repentance and its fruits needed only more remotely. He urges believers to expect full sanctification by faith, as they are, and now.
sermons.context: The Bicentennial editor places the sermon after Wesley's controversy with followers of Robert Sandeman over faith and assurance, at a time of unsettled views among the Methodists. The editor calls it 'the most successful summary of the Wesleyan vision of the ordo salutis in the entire sermon corpus'. He counts forty uses of Ephesians 2:8 in Wesley's oral preaching before 1765 and five further editions in Wesley's lifetime.
sermons.key_line: The end is, in one word, salvation; the means to attain it, faith.

sermons.title: On the Death of the Rev. Mr. George Whitefield
sermons.place: Chapel in Tottenham Court Road, London (repeated at the Tabernacle, Moorfields, 23 November 1770)
sermons.occasion: Funeral sermon for George Whitefield, who died at Newburyport, Massachusetts, on 30 September 1770
sermons.published_in: Published separately (five editions in two years, per the Bicentennial editor); omitted from Sermons on Several Occasions (1787–88); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 53; Bicentennial Works 2:325–347
sermons.summary: Taking Balaam's wish to 'die the death of the righteous', Wesley outlines Whitefield's life and death, drawing largely on Whitefield's own journals and on excerpts from the Boston Gazette and the London Evening Post. He then describes Whitefield's character, including his capacity for 'the most tender friendship' and his 'catholic love' for all whom he believed to be children of God. He urges hearers to hold to the doctrines Whitefield preached, which he sums up as the new birth and justification by faith, and to share his spirit of love.
sermons.context: John Gillies's Memoirs of Whitefield records that whenever Whitefield's friend Mr Keen asked who should preach his funeral sermon if he died abroad, Whitefield answered that Wesley was the man. Keen therefore engaged Wesley on 10 November 1770. The Bicentennial editor calls the occasion awkward: three months earlier Wesley's Conference had issued a warning against leaning toward Calvinism, and the breach over 'Free Grace' had never fully healed. Wesley's Journal says most of the congregation appeared deeply affected; at the Tabernacle, where he was due to begin at half past five, the building was full by three, so he began at four.
sermons.key_line: How few have we known of so kind a temper, of such large and flowing affections!

sermons.title: On Charity
sermons.published_in: Arminian Magazine VIII (1785), 8–16 and 70–76, untitled as 'Sermon XXV'; Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. VII (1788); Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 91; Bicentennial Works 3:290–307
sermons.summary: Wesley argues that Paul's Greek word agape means love, and that the 'charity' of 1 Corinthians 13 is love of neighbour flowing from love of God, which itself springs from faith in Christ. He describes its marks and lists what people commonly put in its place: eloquence, knowledge, faith, good works and suffering. He maintains that none of these, alone or together, can supply the want of love.
sermons.context: The Bicentennial editor notes that Wesley used this text for about a dozen oral sermons in 1784, and again eight times in 1785 and three times in 1787. A hearer's manuscript summary survives in Drew University Library of a 'Charity Sermon' on 1 Corinthians 13:3. Wesley preached it at St John's, Clerkenwell, on 16 December 1787, and the editor says it is close to this written text.
sermons.key_line: St. Paul's word is agape, exactly answering to the plain English word love.

sermons.title: On Friendship with the World
sermons.place: Wakefield (where Wesley finished and dated the text)
sermons.published_in: Arminian Magazine IX (August 1786), 404–17, untitled as 'Sermon XXXIII'; Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. VI; Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 80; Bicentennial Works 3:126–140
sermons.summary: Wesley reads 'the world' in James 4:4 as the people who neither love nor fear God. Christians should love them, speak kindly of them and do them good, but should not form close friendships with them, least of all through marriage. He argues that such intimacy is a sin in itself and slowly corrupts the believer's heart. He answers common reasons given for it (learning, good nature, usefulness in business, family ties) and calls Methodists to avoid it.
sermons.context: The Bicentennial editor, drawing on Wesley's Journal and diary, records that Wesley finished the sermon at Wakefield on the morning of 1 May 1786 before leaving for Leeds. It appeared whole in a single issue of the Arminian Magazine, the only Wesley sermon printed that way. The editor notes Wesley had preached on James 4:4 only once before (London, 11 December 1784) and links the sermon's warnings to Methodists' growing respectability and wealth.
sermons.key_line: Have no friendship with the world.

sermons.title: The Duty of Reproving Our Neighbour
sermons.published_in: Arminian Magazine XI (January–February 1788), untitled as 'Sermon XLIII'; Sermons on Several Occasions, vol. V; Jackson ed. (1872) Sermon 65; Bicentennial Works 2:511–520
sermons.summary: Reading Leviticus 19:17 as setting rebuke against hatred, Wesley treats reproving a neighbour's sin as a duty of love owed to everyone, and especially to those to whom it is particularly due, such as parents, spouses, children, other relatives and servants. Reproof should be given in a spirit of love, humility and meekness, with prayer and at suitable times, and rarely over matters that are genuinely open to dispute. He closes by telling Methodists that he never heard or read of any considerable revival of religion that was not attended with a spirit of reproving.
sermons.context: The Bicentennial editor records that the sermon was written in July 1787 and printed in the Arminian Magazine early in 1788. The only recorded instances of Wesley preaching on Leviticus 19:17 are in 1784 and 1787. The editor links its theme to Puritan precedents, including Richard Baxter and a sermon in the collection edited by Wesley's grandfather Samuel Annesley.
sermons.key_line: Anger, though it be adorned with the name of zeal, begets anger; not love or holiness.
